name: Hosea
sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew Masoretic Text as given in the Westminster Leningrad Codex (Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible edition). Hosea’s Hebrew is among the most difficult in the Old Testament, perhaps reflecting a northern dialect as well as damage in transmission, and many lines are uncertain; significant difficulties are footnoted. The Septuagint (Old Greek) has been consulted throughout. Hosea is the first of the Twelve Prophets (the “Minor Prophets”), which were copied together on a single scroll in antiquity. Among the Dead Sea Scrolls, as reported in the published editions, the Hebrew manuscripts of the Twelve from Qumran (including 4QXII-a, one of the oldest, and 4QXII-c, d, and g, which preserve parts of Hosea) and the Greek Minor Prophets Scroll from Nahal Hever (8HevXIIgr), a Jewish revision of the Septuagint toward the Hebrew, generally support the Masoretic Text. Verse numbers follow the standard English numbering, which differs from the Hebrew in three places: English 1:10–11 is Hebrew 2:1–2, so English 2:1–23 is Hebrew 2:3–25; English 11:12 is Hebrew 12:1, so English 12:1–14 is Hebrew 12:2–15; and English 13:16 is Hebrew 14:1, so English 14:1–9 is Hebrew 14:2–10.

verses.text: The word of Yahweh that came to Hosea{a} son of Beeri in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash,{b} king of Israel.

When Yahweh first spoke through Hosea, Yahweh said to Hosea, “Go, take for yourself a wife of whoredom and have children of whoredom,{c} for the land commits great whoredom by turning away from Yahweh.”
So he went and took Gomer daughter of Diblaim, and she conceived and bore him a son.
Yahweh said to him, “Name him Jezreel,{d} because a little while more and I will avenge the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu, and I will bring the kingdom of the house of Israel to an end.
On that day I will break the bow of Israel in the Valley of Jezreel.”
She conceived again and bore a daughter, and he said to him, “Call her name Lo-ruhamah,{e} for I will no longer show compassion to the house of Israel, that I should in any way forgive them.
But to the house of Judah I will show compassion, and I will save them by Yahweh their God; I will not save them by bow or sword or warfare, by horses or horsemen.”
When she had weaned Lo-ruhamah, she conceived and bore a son.
And he said, “Call his name Lo-ammi,{f} for you are not my people, and I am not your I AM.”{g}

Yet the number of the children of Israel{h} shall be like sand by the sea, which no one can measure or count; and in the very place where they were told, “You are not my people,” they shall be called, “Children of the living God.”{i}
And the people of Judah and the people of Israel will be gathered together, and they will appoint for themselves one head, and they will go up from the land, for great will be the day of Jezreel.

notes.text: The name means “salvation” or “he has saved,” from the same root as Joshua and Isaiah.
Hebrew Yoʾash, a variant spelling of Jehoash. Jeroboam II reigned about 786–746 BC; Hosea’s ministry began in his last years and continued after the fall of his dynasty (compare 1:4).

Hebrew zenunim, “promiscuity, fornication,” used throughout Hosea as a figure for Israel’s worship of other gods (especially Baal) and for its political alliances. Whether Gomer was unfaithful before the marriage or only afterward (looking back from its outcome) is debated.

The name means “God sows.” Jezreel was the town and valley where Jehu wiped out the house of Ahab (2 Kings 9–10). Jehu’s dynasty ended when his great-great-grandson Zechariah, son of Jeroboam II, was assassinated in about 746 BC (2 Kings 15:8–12). In 2:22–23 the name is turned to promise: God will “sow” Israel in the land.
The name means “not pitied” or “shown no compassion.”
The name means “not my people.”
Hebrew loʾ-ʾehyeh lakem, “I am not ‘I AM’ to you,” echoing the divine name revealed in Exodus 3:14 (“I AM WHO I AM”). Most translations render “I am not your God,” following the sense.
Verses 10–11 are 2:1–2 in the Hebrew text.
Quoted in Romans 9:26.

verses.text: Say to your brothers, “Ammi,”{a} and to your sisters, “Ruhamah.”

“Contend with your mother, contend—
for she is no wife of mine,
and I am no husband of hers—
and let her remove her harlotry from her face,
her adulteries from between her breasts,

lest I strip her bare
and set her out as on the day of her birth,
make her like the wilderness,
leave her like a land of drought,
and let her die of thirst.

Upon her children also I will have no compassion,
because they are children of whoredom.

For their mother has played the whore;
she who conceived them has acted shamefully.
For she said, ‘I will go after my lovers,
who give me my bread and my water,
my wool and my flax, my oil and my drinks.’

Therefore I am going to hedge up her{b} way with thorns,
and I will build a wall against her,
so that she cannot find her paths.

She will pursue her lovers but not overtake them;
she will search for them but not find them.
Then she will say, ‘Let me go back to my first husband,
for it was better with me then than it is now.’

She did not acknowledge that it was I who gave her
the grain, the new wine, and the oil,
and lavished on her silver,
and gold that they made into Baal.{c}

Therefore I will take back my grain in its time,
and my new wine in its season;
I will snatch away my wool and my flax,
which were to cover her nakedness.

Now I will uncover her shame{d} in the sight of her lovers,
and no one will rescue her out of my hand.

I will make all her merriment cease,
her feasts, her new moons, and her Sabbaths,
every one of her appointed times.

I will lay waste her vines and her fig trees,
of which she said, ‘These are my wages,
which my lovers have given me.’
I will make them a thicket,
and the beasts of the field will devour them.

I will call her to account for the days of the Baals,
when she offered incense to them,
decked herself with her ring and her necklace,
and went after her lovers,
but forgot me,” declares Yahweh.

“Therefore, look, I am going to allure her
and lead her into the wilderness,
and speak to her heart.

From there I will give back her vineyards to her,
and make the Valley of Achor{e} a doorway of hope.
And there she shall respond as in the days of her youth,
as in the day when she came up out of the land of Egypt.

For I will remove the names of the Baals from her mouth,
and they will be remembered by name no more.

On that day I will make a covenant for them
with the beasts of the field, the birds of the heavens,
and the creeping things of the ground.
Bow and sword and war I will break and banish from the land,
and I will make them lie down in safety.

I will betroth you to me in faithfulness,
and you will know Yahweh.

the earth will answer the grain, the new wine, and the oil,
and they will answer Jezreel.{g}

notes.text: That is, “my people” and “pitied.” Verses 1–23 are 2:3–25 in the Hebrew text.
Hebrew “your”; the Septuagint and Syriac read “her.”
Or “that they used for Baal.” Baal was the Canaanite storm god, believed to give rain and fertility.
Hebrew naḇluth, a rare word, perhaps “lewdness” or “genitals.”
The name means “trouble,” recalling the sin of Achan (Joshua 7:24–26).
Hebrew ʾishi, “my man, my husband,” and baʿli, “my master, my husband,” a word identical with the name of the god Baal.
Here the name keeps its meaning, “God sows.”
Quoted in Romans 9:25 and echoed in 1 Peter 2:10.

verses.text: Yahweh said to me, “Go once more and love a woman, loved by a lover{a} and committing adultery, even as Yahweh loves the children of Israel, though they look to other gods and love raisin cakes.”{b}
So I bought her for myself for fifteen pieces of silver and about nine bushels of barley.{c}
And I said to her, “You are to dwell as mine for many days. You shall not play the whore or belong to another man; and I also will be toward you.”{d}
For many days the children of Israel shall remain with no king and no prince, with no sacrifice and no pillar, with no ephod and no household gods.{e}
Afterward the people of Israel will return and seek Yahweh their God and David their king, and they will come trembling to Yahweh and to his goodness in the latter days.

notes.text: Or “loved by a husband” or “loves a companion.” Most take the woman to be Gomer; some think she is another woman.
Probably offerings used in pagan worship (compare Jeremiah 7:18; 44:19).

Hebrew “a homer of barley and a lethech of barley,” a homer and a half-homer (about 330 liters). The silver was probably fifteen shekels (about 6 ounces or 170 grams). The Septuagint has “a homer of barley and a skin of wine.”
The Hebrew is terse; it may mean “so will I also be to you” or “and I too will not come to you.”
Hebrew teraphim. The pillar (matsseḇah) was a standing stone used in worship; the ephod was a priestly garment used to seek oracles.

verses.text:
Hear the word of Yahweh, children of Israel,
for Yahweh has a dispute{a} with those who live in the land:
no truth is there, no steadfast love,
no knowledge of God in the land.

Swearing and deceiving, killing and theft and adultery—they burst all bounds,
and blood touches blood.

Therefore the land mourns,
and all who dwell in it languish,
along with the beasts of the field and the birds of the heavens;
even the fish of the sea are swept away.

By day you shall stumble,
and by night the prophet shall stumble beside you,
and I will make your mother perish.

My people perish for want of knowledge.
Since you have spurned knowledge,
I spurn you from serving me as priest;
since you forgot your God’s instruction,
your sons I too will forget.

The more they increased, the more they sinned against me;
I will change their glory into disgrace.{c}

On my people’s sin they feed,
and to their iniquity they lift up their appetite.

And it will be: like people, like priest.
I will punish them for their ways
and repay them for their deeds.

to whoredom.
Wine and new wine take away the understanding.{d}

On the tops of the mountains they sacrifice,
and on the hills they burn offerings,
under oak, poplar, and terebinth,
because their shade is good.
Therefore your daughters play the whore,
and your daughters-in-law commit adultery.

For like a stubborn heifer,
Israel is stubborn;
can Yahweh now pasture them
like a lamb in a broad meadow?

Ephraim is joined to idols;
leave him alone.

When their drinking is over,{g} they give themselves to whoring;
her rulers dearly love shame.

A wind has wrapped them{h} in its wings,
and they will be ashamed because of their sacrifices.

notes.text: Hebrew riḇ, a legal dispute or lawsuit.
The Hebrew is difficult; literally “and your people are like those who contend with a priest.”
An ancient scribal tradition (one of the “corrections of the scribes”) says the original read “they exchanged my glory for disgrace.”
Hebrew “the heart,” the seat of thought.
Hebrew qedeshot, “consecrated women,” probably women attached to a shrine; the exact nature of their role is debated.
Beth-aven, “house of wickedness,” is a mocking name for Bethel, “house of God” (compare 5:8; 10:5; Amos 5:5).
Or “Their liquor is gone” or “Their drink has turned sour.” The Hebrew of verse 18 is very uncertain.
Hebrew “her.”

verses.text:
Rebels have gone deep into slaughter,{a}
but I am a rebuke to them all.

Blow the horn in Gibeah,
the trumpet in Ramah!
Raise the cry at Beth-aven:
“Behind you, Benjamin!”{d}

Ephraim shall be a desolation
in the day of rebuke;
among the tribes of Israel
I make known what is sure.

Ephraim is crushed and oppressed, broken by judgment,
for he willingly walked after filth.{e}

So I am like a moth to Ephraim,
and like rot to the house of Judah.

When Ephraim saw his sickness,
and Judah his wound,
Ephraim went to Assyria
and sent to the great king.{f}
But he is not able to heal you
or cure you of your wound.

For I will be like a lion to Ephraim,
and like a young lion to the house of Judah.
I, even I, will tear and go away;
I will carry off, and none shall rescue.

notes.text: The Hebrew of this line is obscure; some, with a change of letters, read “they have made deep the pit of Shittim.”
Ephraim, the largest tribe of the north, is Hosea’s usual name for the northern kingdom of Israel.
Or “a month shall devour them with their portions.” The meaning is uncertain.
Verses 8–14 probably reflect the Syro-Ephraimite war of about 734–732 BC (2 Kings 16:5–9; Isaiah 7).
Hebrew tsaw, of uncertain meaning; perhaps “a command” or a mocking word for idols. The Septuagint reads “vanities.”
Hebrew melek yareḇ, traditionally “King Jareb.” With a different division of the letters, malki raḇ, it is the Assyrian royal title “the great king.” Likewise at 10:6.

verses.text:
Ephraim, what am I to do with you?
Judah, what am I to do with you?
Your loyalty is like mist at morning,
like dew that vanishes early.

For I delight in steadfast love{c} and not sacrifice,
in the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.

But they, like Adam,{d} broke the covenant;
there they betrayed me.

Gilead is a town of evildoers,
tracked with blood.

In the house of Israel I have seen a horrible thing;
Ephraim’s harlotry is there; Israel is defiled.

For you also, Judah, a harvest is appointed,
when I restore the fortunes of my people.

notes.text: A poetic way of saying “very soon.” Early Christian writers saw here a foreshadowing of the resurrection of Christ on the third day (compare 1 Corinthians 15:4).
So the Septuagint and Syriac, by a different division of the letters; the Hebrew reads “and your judgments are light that goes out.”
Hebrew ḥeseḏ, loyal, covenant love. The Septuagint has “mercy”; Jesus quotes this verse in Matthew 9:13 and 12:7.
Or “like mortals” or (with a change of one letter) “at Adam,” a town in the Jordan valley (Joshua 3:16), which would suit “there.”

verses.text:
But they do not say in their hearts
that I remember all their wickedness.
Now their deeds surround them;
they are before my face.

With their wickedness they make the king glad,
and the princes with their lies.

They are all adulterers;
they are like an oven heated by the baker,
who ceases to stir the fire
from the kneading of the dough until it is leavened.

On the day of our king the princes made themselves sick with the heat of wine;
he stretched out his hand with scoffers.

Ephraim mixes himself among the peoples;
Ephraim is a flat cake not turned.

Strangers devour his strength,
and he does not know it;
gray hairs are sprinkled upon him,
and he does not know it.

Woe to them, for they have wandered away from me!
Ruin upon them, for they have revolted against me!
I would ransom them,
yet they tell lies about me.

Though I trained and strengthened their arms,
yet against me they devise evil.

They turn, but not upward;{e}
they are like a slack bow.
Their princes shall fall by the sword
because of the insolence of their tongue.
This shall be their derision in the land of Egypt.

notes.text: So the Syriac and Targum; the Hebrew reads “their baker.”
Hebrew “their judges.” In the last years of the northern kingdom four of its six kings were assassinated (2 Kings 15).
The Hebrew of this line is uncertain.
So some Hebrew manuscripts and the Septuagint; most manuscripts read “they gather themselves together.” Gashing the body was a rite of Baal worship (1 Kings 18:28).
Hebrew loʾ ʿal, “not up,” obscure; perhaps “not to the Most High” or “to what does not profit.”

verses.text:
Set the horn to your mouth!
Like a vulture{a} one comes upon Yahweh’s house,
since they have broken my covenant
and defied my instruction.

To me they cry,
“My God, we—Israel—know you.”

Israel has spurned what is good;
the enemy shall pursue him.

They have crowned kings, but not by my will;
they have appointed princes, but without my knowledge.
Of their silver and gold they have fashioned idols
to their own cutting off.

For this thing too is out of Israel;
a workman fashioned it,
and it is not God.
Samaria’s calf
will be smashed to pieces.

Though they hire them among the nations,
now I will gather them up.
And they shall soon writhe
under the burden of the king of princes.{c}

Ephraim made many altars to take away sin,
but they became altars for committing sin.

Though I write for him my laws by the ten thousand,
they are regarded as a strange thing.

For Israel has forgotten his Maker
and built palaces,
and Judah has multiplied fortified cities;
but I will send a fire upon his cities,
and it shall devour her strongholds.

notes.text: Or “eagle.” “The house of Yahweh” here may mean the land or people of Israel.
The golden calf set up by Jeroboam I at Bethel (1 Kings 12:28–30). The Hebrew may also be read as a command: “Reject your calf, Samaria.”
Probably the Assyrian king. The Septuagint reads “they shall cease for a little while from anointing a king and princes.”

verses.text:
Rejoice not, Israel,
exult not like the peoples;
for you have played the harlot, forsaking your God.
You have loved a harlot’s wages
on all the threshing floors of grain.

Threshing floor and winepress shall not feed them,
and the new wine shall fail her.

What will you do on the solemn day,
the day of Yahweh’s festival?

The days of reckoning have come,
the days of payment are here;
let Israel know it!
“The prophet is a fool,
the man of the spirit is out of his mind!”—
so great is your iniquity,
so great your hostility.

I found Israel
like grapes in the desert;
like the early fruit on a fig tree
at its first bearing
I looked on your ancestors.
But they went to Baal-peor{c}
and dedicated themselves to the Shameful Thing,
and they became as loathsome as the thing they loved.

Like a bird Ephraim’s glory will fly off—
no childbirth, no womb, no conceiving!

Though they raise sons,
I will rob them of them until not one remains.
Woe to them indeed
when I turn away from them!

Ephraim, as I have seen, was like Tyre,{d} planted in a meadow;
but Ephraim must lead out his children to slaughter.

Give them, Yahweh—
what will you give?
Give them a miscarrying womb
and dry breasts.

notes.text: Hebrew Moph, the ancient capital of Lower Egypt, near modern Cairo, famous for its necropolis.
See Judges 19–21.
See Numbers 25:1–5. “The Shameful Thing” (Hebrew bosheth) is a common substitute for the name Baal.
The Hebrew of this line is uncertain.
Gilgal was a major sanctuary (4:15; 12:11; Amos 4:4) and the place where Saul was made king (1 Samuel 11:15).

verses.text:
Their heart is false;{b}
now they must bear their guilt.
He himself will break down their altars
and wreck their pillars.

For soon they will say,
“We have no king,
because we did not fear Yahweh;
and a king—what could he do for us?”

For the calf{c} of Beth-aven
the people of Samaria tremble.
Its people mourn over it,
and its idol-priests{d} writhe over it,
over its glory, because it has departed from them into exile.

The thing itself will be carried to Assyria
as tribute to the great king.{e}
Ephraim will be put to shame,
and Israel will be disgraced for his counsel.

Samaria and her king are swept off{f}
like a chip on the face of the waters.

The high places of Aven,{g} the sin of Israel,
will be wiped out.
Thorn and thistle will climb over their altars,
and they will say to the mountains, “Cover us,”
and to the hills, “Fall on us.”{h}

the din of war shall rise against your people,
and every fortress of yours shall be ruined,
as Shalman{n} ruined Beth-arbel in the day of battle,
when the mother was dashed to pieces upon her children.

So it shall be done to you, Bethel,
because of your utter wickedness.
At daybreak the king of Israel
will be cut off completely.

notes.text: Or “a luxuriant vine”; the Hebrew boqeq can also mean “empty” or “ravaged.”
Or “divided” or “slippery.”
So the Septuagint; the Hebrew has the feminine plural, “calves,” perhaps in mockery.
Hebrew kemarim, a word used only of priests of false gods (2 Kings 23:5; Zephaniah 1:4).
See the note at 5:13.
Or “Samaria’s king is destroyed.”
That is, Beth-aven (Bethel); aven means “wickedness.”
Quoted in Luke 23:30 and echoed in Revelation 6:16.
The Hebrew of this line is obscure.
So a Hebrew reading (Qere); the written text (Kethiv) may mean “their two springs” or “their two eyes.”
Hebrew “I passed over the goodness of her neck.” Threshing was light work, and the ox was free to eat while it worked (Deuteronomy 25:4).
Or “teaches you righteousness”; the Hebrew verb yarah can mean both “to rain” and “to teach.” The Septuagint reads “until the fruits of righteousness come to you.”
So the Hebrew; the Septuagint reads “in your chariots.”
Perhaps Shalmaneser V of Assyria (727–722 BC) or Salamanu, a king of Moab mentioned in Assyrian records. Neither the event nor the location of Beth-arbel is otherwise known.

verses.text:
When Israel was a youth, I loved him,
and from Egypt I summoned my son.{a}

The more they{b} called them,
the farther they went from them;{c}
they kept sacrificing to the Baals
and burning offerings to carved images.

notes.text: Israel as God’s son recalls Exodus 4:22–23. The Septuagint reads “I called his children.” Matthew 2:15 quotes the line, following the Hebrew, of the return of the child Jesus from Egypt, seeing in Jesus the one who sums up and fulfills Israel’s history.
The Septuagint reads “I.”
The Septuagint reads “from me.”
So the Septuagint, Syriac, and Vulgate; the Hebrew reads “his.”
Or, with different vowels, “as those who lift an infant to their cheeks.”
Or, joining the word to verse 4, “to him. They will return…”
Or “their boasters” or “their oracle-priests”; Hebrew baddim.
Or “they are called to the yoke”; the Hebrew of this line is uncertain.
Two cities destroyed together with Sodom and Gomorrah (Deuteronomy 29:23).
Or “I will not come into the city.”
Verse 12 is 12:1 in the Hebrew text.
Or “roams unruly against God.” The Hebrew verb is uncertain.
Or “holy ones.”

verses.text:
In the womb he grabbed his brother’s heel,{b}
and in his manhood he strove with God.

Yahweh, the God of Armies,{e}
Yahweh is his name!{f}

A trader, with false scales in his hand,
he loves to defraud.{g}

By a prophet Yahweh brought Israel up from Egypt,
and by a prophet he was kept.{k}

notes.text: Verses 1–14 are 12:2–15 in the Hebrew text.
The name Jacob sounds like the Hebrew word for “heel” (Genesis 25:26). For the struggle with God, see Genesis 32:22–32; the name Israel was explained as “he strives with God.”
Or “He found him at Bethel” (Genesis 28:10–22; 35:1–15).
So the Hebrew; the Septuagint and Syriac read “with him.”
Hebrew YHWH ʾelohe hatstseḇaʾoth, traditionally “the LORD God of hosts,” the God who commands the armies of heaven and of Israel.
Hebrew zikro, “his memorial,” the name by which he is to be remembered (Exodus 3:15).
Hebrew kenaʿan, “Canaan,” which also means “merchant.”
Probably the Feast of Booths, when Israel lived in temporary shelters (Leviticus 23:42–43).
There are wordplays in Hebrew between Gilead, Gilgal, and gallim, “heaps.”
See Genesis 28:5; 29:1–30.
That is, Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15; 34:10).

verses.text:
Therefore they will be like the morning mist,
like dew that soon passes away,
like chaff swirled from the threshing floor,
like smoke from a window.{b}

It was I who knew you{d} in the wilderness,
in the land of burning drought.

So to them I am become a lion;
I will watch by the way like a leopard.

It is your destruction, Israel,
that you are against me, against your help.{f}

Where now is your king, to save you in all your cities?
Where are your rulers{g}
of whom you said,
“Give me a king and princes”?

I keep giving you a king in my anger
and taking him away in my fury.

The iniquity of Ephraim is tied up in a bundle;
his sin is stored away.

Labor pains are coming upon him,
yet he is a son without wisdom,
for at the right time he does not come forth
to the place where children are born.

Though he flourishes among his brothers,{j}
an east wind will come,
the wind of Yahweh rising from the desert,
and his spring will dry up,
his fountain run dry;
it will plunder his treasury
of every precious thing.

notes.text: Or “They say to them, ‘Sacrifice!’ Men kiss calves.” The Hebrew is uncertain; kissing an idol was an act of homage (1 Kings 19:18).
That is, from an opening in the roof or wall through which smoke escaped.
The Septuagint here adds a long passage on God as creator of heaven and earth.
The Septuagint and Syriac read “who fed you,” a difference of one letter.
Hebrew “the enclosure of their heart.”
The Hebrew is uncertain. The Septuagint and Syriac read “I will destroy you, Israel; who will help you?”
Hebrew “your judges.” For the request, see 1 Samuel 8:5–6.
The realm of the dead. The first two lines may also be read as statements: “I will ransom them … I will redeem them.”
Paul quotes these lines, following the Septuagint, in 1 Corinthians 15:55: “O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?”
There is a wordplay between yaphriʾ, “flourishes,” and the name Ephraim.
Verse 16 is 14:1 in the Hebrew text. Samaria fell to the Assyrians in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:5–6).

verses.text:
Return, Israel, to Yahweh your God,{a}
for your iniquity has made you stumble.

Bring words with you
as you return to Yahweh.
Say to him:
“Take every iniquity away,
receive us graciously,
and we will offer the fruit of our lips.{b}

Who is wise? Let him grasp these things.
Who is discerning? Let him know them.
For straight are the ways of Yahweh;
the righteous walk in them,
but in them transgressors stumble.

notes.text: Verses 1–9 are 14:2–10 in the Hebrew text.
So the Septuagint and Syriac; the Hebrew reads “we will pay bulls, our lips,” meaning that praise will take the place of sacrifices (compare Hebrews 13:15).
Hebrew “like Lebanon”; likewise in verses 6 and 7.
Or “they will revive like grain.”
Or “Ephraim will say, ‘What more have I to do with idols?’ ”
